extracted.intended_audience: model aeroplane designers, competition entrants, and hobbyist aeronautical engineers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and descriptive criteria for designing, building, and judging small rubber-powered model aeroplanes that compete in open competitions; emphasizes features that affect stability, control, efficiency, and flight performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: M.E.P. estimation rule
rubrics_metrics.description: "Add 14·7 to gauge pressure of boiler, this giving 'absolute steam pressure,' multiply this sum by the number opposite the fraction representing the point of cut-off in the cylinder in accompanying table. Subtract 17 from the product and multiply the remainder by 0·9. The result will be very nearly the M.E.P." (R.M. de Vignier.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A step-by-step arithmetic rule to estimate the Mean Effective Pressure (M.E.P.) from gauge pressure and cut-off fraction; presented as an approximate practical calculation method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability (competition scoring)
rubrics_metrics.description: This machine "has always gained very high marks for stability."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stability is a primary judging metric in competitions. Design choices affecting stability mentioned include dihedral angles, fin placement, ailerons (removed because they retarded speed), canting the elevator for steering, and general mass distribution and construction quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directional control / steering
rubrics_metrics.description: Steering of the model is effected by canting the elevator. Some models use rudders and keels; twin propellers have been tried to obtain more directional control but with little, if any, success.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designers should consider elevator canting, rudder/keel placement, and fin geometry to achieve directional certainty; twin propellers are not necessarily effective. Rear rudder and keel below the centre of gravity are cited as control elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propeller size and proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: The large size of the propeller should be noted; the author is in complete agreement. (Example: propeller diameter 56 per cent. of the span.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large-diameter propellers are recommended for efficiency and performance; small propellers are explicitly 'in total disagreement with the author's ideas.' Designers should note propeller-to-span ratio as an important parameter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supporting area efficiency (lift loading)
rubrics_metrics.description: Their efficiency, so far as their supporting area goes, is of the highest, as much as 21 oz. per square foot having been carried.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supporting area (wing area) should be sized to carry intended payload; the oz-per-square-foot figure is provided as an empirical efficiency measure for judging supporting capability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aerofoil shape and construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of various aerofoil shapes: triangular-shaped aerofoils with umbrella ribs and piano wire trailing edges, and later aerofoils of the elongated ellipse shape; shapes resembling certain successful monoplane types.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aerofoil profile and construction method affect lift and durability. Some designs include mechanisms to allow the front plane to partially detach on collision to reduce damage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aspect ratio
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aspect ratio is reported for competing models and is a design variable affecting lift, drag, and performance; include it among specifications when evaluating a design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight, dimensions, and weight-to-area considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Example model particulars: Weight, 7½ oz. Area of supporting surface, 1-1/3 sq. ft. Total length, 4 ft. Span of main aerofoil, 25 in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Absolute weight, wing area, span, and their ratios are used to evaluate flight potential; lighter gearing and optimized structural weight contribute to longer flights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rubber motor and gearing specification
rubrics_metrics.description: Two strand geared rubber motor, carrying altogether 28 strands of 1/16 square rubber cord 43 in. long. Small amount of rubber carried for a long distance machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Motor capacity (number and size/length of rubber strands) and gearing design should be matched to model weight and desired flight profile; minimizing gearing weight and friction is important for distance designs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gearing and friction minimization
rubrics_metrics.description: The weight of which (gearing mechanism) was reduced to a minimum; allowance must be made for friction in gearing, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reducing gearing weight and friction directly improves flight duration and distance; designers should minimize mass and friction in transmission components.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protective skid and undercarriage design
rubrics_metrics.description: The front skid of steel pianoforte wire, the rear of jointless cane wire tipped; the rear skid was a necessity in order to protect the delicate gearing mechanism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under-carriage/skid design should protect vulnerable components (gearing) on landing or rough ground; materials and tip design are practical considerations for survivability and repeated flights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fin placement for transverse stability and directional control
rubrics_metrics.description: The fin, high above the centre of gravity, was so placed for transverse stability and direction. At the rear of the fin was a rudder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vertical surfaces placed above the centre of gravity can enhance transverse stability; pairing a high fin with a rear rudder is recommended for directional authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collision survivability (detachable front plane)
rubrics_metrics.description: A neat little device enabling the front plane to become partly detached on collision with any obstacle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate sacrificial or detachable attachments on forward lifting surfaces to reduce structural damage in collisions, aiding longevity and repeated competition entries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and quality of construction
rubrics_metrics.description: The model is 'a thoroughly well designed and well constructed model.' Originally a very slow flyer, the design has been simplified, and although by no means a fast flyer, its speed has been much accelerated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simplicity in design and high construction quality correlate with better competition outcomes. Removal of speed-retarding components (e.g., ailerons) and simplification can improve flight speed and reliability. Note: one illustrated design is patented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flight performance metrics (distance, duration, straightness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Competition performance examples: flown over 300 yards; best flight 320 yards measured in straight line; duration of flight 50 seconds; best and straightest flight against the wind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Competitions assess distance (yards), duration (seconds), and ability to fly straight against wind; designers should optimize for these measurable outcomes and record such metrics for evaluation.
